content:
Talks between the parties of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and prime minister-designate Gadi Eisenkot on forming a unity government ended without a deal on Sunday, leaving Israel's political deadlock unresolved with just two weeks left on Eisenkot's mandate to form a government.

Delegations from Netanyahu's Likud party and Eisenkot's Yashar party met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, in a second round of discussions after an initial meeting the previous weekend, according to [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/netanyahus-likud-eisenkots-yashar-end-coalition-talks-without-deal). In a joint statement, the two sides said they had "outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues" and that "a follow-up meeting would be held", without giving a date or any further details.

The negotiators remained split on the two questions that have defined the standoff since October's inconclusive elections: who will lead the next government, and whether far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir will be part of it. According to Israel's Channel 12 broadcaster, Likud insisted that Ben-Gvir join any unity government, while Yashar demanded his exclusion. The Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported the same divide, with Ben-Gvir's presence emerging as a red line for Eisenkot's camp.

The leadership question proved just as intractable. Yashar, which holds 21 seats in the 120-member Knesset, insists that Eisenkot serve as prime minister for the full term. Likud, with 27 seats, demands that Netanyahu take the premiership first, proposing a rotation of the post between the two men. Eisenkot has opposed a rotation, and Netanyahu has reportedly insisted on going first.

A compromise floated by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together list, would bring Together, Yashar, Likud and Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu into a single coalition, with Eisenkot serving first and Netanyahu succeeding him. But the proposal appears to satisfy neither of the two main parties: Eisenkot rejects rotation outright, while Lieberman has ruled out joining any government that includes Netanyahu at all.

Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after President Isaac Herzog tasked him on November 8 with forming an administration. October's elections gave his four-party bloc 48 seats — Yashar's 21, Together's 12, the Democrats' eight and Yisrael Beiteinu's seven — 13 short of the 61 needed for a majority in the Knesset.

His bloc remains divided over how to close that gap. One route would be an alliance with the ultra-Orthodox parties; another would be a rapprochement with Arab parties; a third is the national unity government with Likud that Netanyahu has been pushing. Each path carries a political cost, and none commands agreement inside the bloc.

If the unity discussions collapse, Yashar plans to seek a confidence vote in the Knesset for a minority government before Eisenkot's mandate expires. A minority administration would depend on outside support from parties unwilling to join the coalition — an arrangement that has rarely proved stable in Israeli politics. If no government is formed by the deadline, the president could pass the mandate to another member of the Knesset, and a further failure could ultimately lead to fresh elections.

The stakes extend well beyond the coalition arithmetic. Netanyahu, who remains caretaker prime minister, has argued that only a unity government can guarantee Israel's security, pointing to the threat from Iran and the fragile Gaza ceasefire. Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff, dismissed Netanyahu's initial invitation to unity talks earlier this month as a "new manoeuvre", and his camp has made clear it will not accept a deal that leaves Netanyahu in charge.

The deadlock also matters for the region. The Gaza ceasefire remains fragile, and [tensions with Iran continue to shape Israeli security policy](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-inclined-resume-iran-strikes-after-new-year-november-2026), with Washington weighing further military action against Tehran in the new year. A caretaker government with no parliamentary majority would struggle to take major decisions on either front, and [debate in the United States over war powers](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-senate-rejects-iran-war-powers-resolution-november-2026) shows how closely Israel's partners are watching the political uncertainty.

For now, both sides say talks will continue, but neither has offered a date for the next round. With the December 6 deadline approaching, the window for a unity deal is narrowing — and the fallback options, a minority government or another election, are ones neither side has shown much appetite for.
summary: Likud and Yashar negotiators met for four hours in Herzliya on Sunday but ended their second round of unity talks without a deal, split over who leads the government and whether far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir joins it, with Gadi Eisenkot's mandate to form a government expiring on December 6.
title: Netanyahu and Eisenkot unity talks end without deal as Israel's government deadlock deepens
